opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I thought it would be vision. I came up through computer vision, and around 2012, when AlexNet won ImageNet, it felt like the whole field suddenly woke up. In the years after that, we kept seeing jumps: detection, segmentation, and then generative models. When GANs appeared and we started generating images that looked real, I remember thinking, okay, this is where the magic is going to happen first. Images are so rich, and the progress you could see with your own eyes was very convincing.

Language felt harder to me at the time. Text is discrete, it's symbolic, and I had the impression that reasoning and understanding language would need some deep structural insight we didn't have yet. So I would have bet on vision, maybe vision combined with robotics, to be the first place where AI felt truly intelligent.

Looking back, I think I underestimated two things. One is how much knowledge is compressed in human text. Language is already an abstraction of the world that people have refined over thousands of years, so a model that learns to predict text inherits a lot of that structure for free. The second is scaling. Once people committed to simple next-token prediction and pushed data and compute much further, the capabilities emerged in a way that surprised many of us, including me.

But I don't think vision lost the race. It's more that language went first because the signal was denser. The physical world is much harder: you have to understand 3D space, dynamics, and causality, and what happens when you push something. That's why I'm so excited about world models and physical AI now. I think the next real breakthrough will come from bringing the generative modeling we learned in vision together with the scaling lessons from language, so machines can understand and act in the real world, not just talk about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he expected vision, possibly combined with robotics, to produce the first breakthrough; it does not say he expected text or language to do so.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I thought it would come from vision first. That was my whole world. I was at NVIDIA Research working on GANs, on image-to-image translation, and the progress in generative vision between 2014 and 2019 felt explosive. Every year the faces got sharper, the resolutions doubled, and I believed the path to something like general intelligence would run through perception. Vision is how humans and animals learn about the world before language. Children see and manipulate objects long before they speak. So it felt natural that if a machine was going to understand the world, it would first learn to see it.

And there was a practical argument too. Images are everywhere. The web gave us essentially unlimited visual data. We had ImageNet, we had strong architectures, we had the hardware. Language, by comparison, seemed harder. Text is discrete, symbolic, and I think many of us in the vision community quietly assumed that real language understanding would require some reasoning machinery we had not invented yet.

What we underestimated was the power of a simple objective at scale. Next-token prediction looks almost trivial. But language turned out to be an incredibly compressed description of the world, written by billions of people, and predicting it well forces the model to learn an enormous amount about how things relate. Vision data is denser, but it is also noisier and less structured. A photo contains a lot of pixels that carry very little meaning.

So when GPT arrived, it was humbling. It did not mean vision was wrong. It meant language had a head start because of how it was packaged. Now I think the two are converging, and the interesting question is how we give models the kind of physical, spatial understanding that language alone cannot provide. That is really where my work has gone since.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he expected vision to produce the first breakthrough; it does not say he expected text or language to lead.

I expected that learning to understand the visual world would be a central step toward intelligence. Language turned out to move much faster than I anticipated.
